content: The term hematology was first used in this country in 1811, but its origins date back further. In 1743, Thomas Schwencke authored Hamatologia, sive Sanguinis Historia, which laid the foundation for the study of blood. Hematology, like bacteriology, has evolved through advancements in laboratory techniques and the application of physics and chemistry. Inflammatory cytokines stimulate the liver to produce increased amounts of hepcidin. Hepcidin inhibits the release of iron from body stores by blocking ferroportin. Additionally, inflammatory cytokines reduce ferroportin expression and impair erythropoiesis by increasing resistance to erythropoietin in the bone marrow. Beyond iron sequestration, inflammatory cytokines promote the production of white blood cells. Since bone marrow stem cells produce both red and white blood cells, the upregulation of white blood cell production reduces the number of stem cells differentiating into red blood cells. This mechanism may contribute to the inhibition of erythropoiesis, even when erythropoietin levels are normal, independent of hepcidin's effects. Furthermore, the half-life of red blood cells is decreased. Conditions such as severe acute infections, trauma, or other inflammatory states, as well as the aging process, can lead to inflammation and anemia. The primary goal in treating anemia of chronic disease (ACD) is to address the underlying disease. Supplemental iron is recommended as needed to maintain transferrin saturation above 20% and serum ferritin levels above 100 ng/mL. Intravenous iron is more effective than oral supplementation. Stable patients may be treated with synthetic erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, such as erythropoietin. Oral iron supplementation should be provided to all patients receiving erythropoietin or darbepoetin to maintain transferrin saturation above 20% and serum ferritin above 100 ng/mL. In severe cases, blood transfusion is recommended. The differentiation between ACD and ACD with concurrent iron deficiency anemia (ACD/IDA) is critical. Soluble transferrin receptor levels (sTfR) and the sTfR-ferritin index are normal in uncomplicated ACD but elevated in cases of ACD/IDA. Additional parameters, such as the percentage of hypochromic red cells and reticulocyte hemoglobin, may aid in distinguishing these conditions. Anemia is present in 30–60% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis and in over 30% of cancer patients, with rates reaching 63% in some cases. Among elderly patients, approximately one-third of anemia cases are attributed to ACD. Risk factors for ACD include autoimmune disorders, chronic infections, trauma, major surgery, malignancy, HIV infection, rheumatologic disorders, inflammatory bowel disease, Castleman disease, heart failure, advanced age, renal insufficiency, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Routine screening for ACD is not recommended due to insufficient evidence. However, age-appropriate health evaluations and assessments of patient symptoms can help identify the underlying cause of ACD. Potentially life-threatening complications of ACD include congestive heart failure, angina, arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, and high-output heart failure. Anemia typically improves when the underlying disease is successfully treated. There is no single diagnostic test for ACD. A detailed medical history may reveal conditions such as autoimmune disorders, chronic infections, trauma, major surgery, malignancy, HIV infection, rheumatologic disorders, inflammatory bowel disease, Castleman disease, heart failure, advanced age, renal insufficiency, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Physical examination findings are usually related to the underlying disease rather than the anemia itself. Laboratory findings in ACD often reveal mild normocytic and normochromic anemia, with hemoglobin concentrations between 10 and 11 g/dL. Less than 25% of cases exhibit microcytic and hypochromic anemia, with a mean corpuscular volume (MCV) below 70 fL. Mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) is normal or low, and red cell distribution width (RDW) is normal to increased. Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) remains unchanged. Severe anemia, with hemoglobin levels below 8 g/dL, occurs in 20% of cases. Absolute reticulocyte counts are often low (<25,000/μL). Elevated levels of cytokines (e.g., IL-6, interferon-gamma) and acute-phase reactants (e.g., fibrinogen, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, ferritin, haptoglobin, factor VIII) may also be observed. An electrocardiogram (ECG) may show left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) in patients with ACD. Chest X-rays are often used to rule out infections in anemic patients. Ultrasound can detect splenomegaly or identify causes of anemia, such as uterine fibroids. CT scans provide detailed images of internal organs and lymph nodes, aiding in the identification of splenomegaly, lymph node abnormalities, or gastrointestinal malignancies causing anemia in patients unable to undergo colonoscopy or endoscopy. MRI is effective for imaging bone and bone marrow disorders and assessing iron concentration in organs such as the heart and liver, particularly in patients with multiple blood transfusions and concerns about iron overload. The primary treatment for ACD is addressing the underlying disease. Supplemental iron is recommended to maintain transferrin saturation above 20% and serum ferritin levels above 100 ng/mL. Intravenous iron is more effective than oral supplementation. Stable patients may receive erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, such as erythropoietin. Oral iron supplementation is essential for patients receiving erythropoietin or darbepoetin to maintain adequate transferrin saturation and serum ferritin levels. In severe cases, blood transfusion is recommended. If the underlying cause is malignancy, chemotherapy or radiotherapy may temporarily worsen anemia due to myelosuppressive effects but ultimately lead to improvement. For inflammatory disorders, such as rheumatoid arthritis, treatment with disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) significantly improves anemia. Surgical intervention is not recommended for managing ACD. There are no established measures for the primary or secondary prevention of ACD.
